correctness.rationale: A rose has a unique degree-2k hub h and all other vertices degree two. C² with counting defines deg=2k at rank 1, and by alternating two variable names defines distance ≤d from that hub with rank ≤d+1. A candidate graph satisfying the exact degree counts and layer histograms through D is connected to h within D. Removing h leaves degree≤2 components; no isolated vertex is possible in a simple graph with other vertices degree two, and no disjoint cycle can lie within a finite hub distance. Thus each component is a path with both endpoints adjacent to h, recovering a rose. At distance d, an even petal 2d has one midpoint with two neighbors at d−1; an odd petal 2d+1 has two midpoint vertices with one same-layer neighbor. Counting these signatures at rank ≤d+3 recovers every petal multiplicity. The finite palette C²-type/histogram characterization yields one rank≤D+3 identifying sentence. For A_r=R(2r+3,2r+7) vs B_r=R(2r+5,2r+5), both order 4r+9 and radius-r degree-rooted unfoldings have the same histogram; C² equivalence holds through rank r+1, yielding lower identifying rank r+2=D−1. Independently verified common-palette colour refinement for r=1..20 and length readout in tested examples. This is finite corroboration, not proof of the all-r indistinguishability.
